messages.subject: Re: regressing out batch effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kylie,

Thank you - this clears up a lot.  The data were indeed from a continuous format imzML.  You have done a very nice job with this package already.  So despite processing the files together after merging, the segmentation is still done separately?  If so, I will just specify ~condition when using segmentation based testing but would then like to map across tissue samples.  Do you have any hints or ways you recommend doing it in addition to those that Olga mentioned?

Thanks,
Nadia

On Wednesday, August 30, 2023 at 5:37:46 PM UTC-4 kbemis wrote:
>
> Hi Nadia,
>
> If the data is from a "continuous" format imzML and the m/z axes don't already match, then that is the best way to do it currently.
>
> If the data is from a "processed" format imzML, then you can manually specify the mass range and resolution in readImzML() so that they match on import.
>
> Making it easier to merge datasets in all cases is on my todo list for next version.
>
> -Kylie
> On Tuesday, August 29, 2023 at 12:54:19 PM UTC-6 nadiaata...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Thank you Olga,
> >
> > I will move forward with the statistical test then.  However, the mapping across tissue sections is definitely a challenge....
> >
> > So what I have been doing to process the various samples is that I read the imzml file from each sample in separately, I then apply mass binning through mzBin() and process() so that the number of rows are the same for each sample (and so that they have the same resolution).  I then use cbind() to bind all the samples together so that the rest of the pre-processing is done on all samples together.  So my understanding is that the m/z match then (unless I am mistaken).  The file size is quite large, but I am working on a high-memory HPC system so it was okay.
> >
> > I am definitely eager to hear whether Kylie has any words of wisdom on this.  I"m trying to get a handle on this now before our dataset becomes MUCH larger :)
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Nadia
> >
> > On Friday, August 18, 2023 at 6:33:21 PM UTC-4 Olga Vitek wrote:
> > > Hi Nadia,
> > >
> > > You are correct, with two caveats. (1) We do not have an automated procedure for mapping segments between tissues. In the past we have done this manually, using the understanding of the experimental context/known markers/available annotations etc. This may be non-trivial. (2) If you pre-process each batch separately, your list of m/z may be different between the batches. (The problem would go away if you could process all the tissues together. But the file size may be too large for that). So you may need to match the m/z between the batches. You can also try to do this manually. Or, I am wondering if Kylie has any words of wisdom regarding that ;-)
> > >
> > > Sorry for not having an easy solution ;-)
> > >
> > > Sincerely
> > > Olga
> > > On Friday, August 18, 2023 at 10:17:30 AM UTC-4 Nadia Atallah wrote:
> > > > Hi Olga,
> > > >
> > > > Thank you for your reply.  This is a really good point.... we cannot be sure that all locations in the tissue and all ions are affected by batch in the same way... and I actually doubt that they are. Since segmentation is performed separately for each tissue section then batch effects should not have an effect on segmentation-based testing to identify ions that change.  So then in this case, when I perform the segmentation-based testing I should be able to just specify the model using ~ condition.  Is this correct?
> > > >
> > > > And then in the means-based testing, I assume that I should specify the model using ~condition + batch?  This will then take into account batch effects when performing the tests?
> > > >
> > > > Lastly, I am very interested in mapping the identified segments between tissues.  I have looked through the Cardinal documentation and don't see a mention of that (or I am missing it).  Would you mind pointing me in the right direction as to where I can find information on how to do this?
> > > >
> > > > Thank you so much for your time,
> > > > Nadia
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday, August 17, 2023 at 9:17:36 PM UTC-4 Olga Vitek wrote:
> > > > > Hi Nadia,
> > > > >
> > > > > Could you clarify why you need to do normalization prior to segmentation? Normally segmentation is performed separately for each tissue section, and is not affected by tissue batches.
> > > > >
> > > > > What you suggest is a constant normalization, where you multiply (or subtract of the log scale) a constant to equalize medians or some other summary of the intensities in each run. Besides not affecting the segmentation, it will assume that all the locations in the tissue and all the ions are effected by the batch in a same way. This is a quite strong assumption.
> > > > >
> > > > > Another option can be to find segments first, map the segments between the tissues, and compare those. These will indeed require between-batch normalization, but at least in can be more region-specific.
> > > > >
> > > > > HTH
> > > > > Olga
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thursday, August 17, 2023 at 3:01:05 PM UTC-4 Nadia Atallah wrote:
> > > > > > I need to deal with some batch effects in our data and am not quite sure what the optimal way to do so would be....  Our experimental design is that we have one treated and one untreated tissue section in each batch, so treatment effects are not confounded by batch effects.  It is clear though in the PCA plots that there are some strong batch effects present and I am thinking that it would be ideal to normalize or batch effect correct prior to performing segmentation analyses.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > One way that I am thinking I could deal with this is that I could model the relationship between ion intensity and batches and then take the residuals as the scaled data and move forward with the remainder of the analyses.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Has anyone done this before? I imagine that I should attempt to remove batch effects after pre-processing is done.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks,
> > > > > > Nadia

messages.subject: A note on plotting speed
messages.body_plain:
Dear Cardinal Users and developers,

I have some questions on the plotting speed. The Cardinal user manual says:

"While plotting spectra should typically be fast for most datasets regardless of data format, plotting images will typically be slower for out-of-memory (file-based) datasets and for MSProcessedImagingExperiment objects in general."

However, I found that plotting spectra is much slower that plotting images.

Here is my tentative test:

The data set is downloaded from MetaSpace: https://metaspace2020.eu/dataset/2023-09-10_07h41m35s :

Here is the data overview:

An object of class 'MSProcessedImagingExperiment'
  <115130 feature, 2000 pixel> imaging dataset
    imageData(1): intensity
    featureData(0):
    pixelData(0):
    metadata(12): spectrum representation ibd binary type ... files name
    run(1): total
    raster dimensions: 50 x 40 x 1
    coord(3): x = 1..50, y = 1..40, z = 1..1
    mass range: 100.0000 to 999.9949
    centroided: FALSE

#1. Test on plotting image speed

system.time({
  image(mse, feature = 1)
})

user  system elapsed
  0.128   0.002   0.129

#2. Test on plotting spectra speed

system.time({
  plot(mse, pixel = 1)
})

 user  system elapsed
 16.855   0.161  17.326

#3. Test on converting sparse matrix to dense matrix

system.time({
  as.matrix(iData(mse[, 1]))
})

user  system elapsed
 16.797   0.064  16.900

You can see that plotting a spectrum is about 130 times slower than plotting an image. The reason is mainly due to the conversion of the sparse matrix to dense matrix.

I have tried with other ways to speed up plotting spectra, e.g., using Matrix package, but I did not see much improvements.

Please note that the test above is on the raw MSI data. (It is much faster for preprocessed MSI data).

I am writing to ask if there are any ways to speed up plotting spectra for the raw MSI data?

Thanks  a lot.

Yonghui Dong

messages.subject: Re: A note on plotting speed
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yonghui,

This is something that I will focus on improving in the next version this fall so that (1) sparsity is retained during plotting and (2) fewer m/z values are stored if they are not necessary. For the time being, you can use the adata() and aindex() accessors to get the underlying m/z and intensity data from the 'sparse_mat' matrix returned by spectra() if you need.

One more thing: METASPACE should not have raw MSI data. METASPACE expects peak-picked and centroided imzML in continuous format. If someone uploaded a raw profile dataset, I would not trust the resulting annotations.

-Kylie

#2. Test on plotting image speed

  image(mse, feature = 1)
})

user  system elapsed

The plotting speed for image is a bit slower, but It is much faster to plot spectra now.

Thanks a lot again.

Best regards,

Yonghui Dong

messages.subject: Visualizing and handling DESI 3D data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I collected some data using a DESI Synapt G2-Si with ion mobility capabilities. I was having such a hard time visualizing the imzmL file until I realized that Cardinal is having a difficult time with the drift time values in the z coordinate.

My questions are:
1) Is there any way to visualize the image using just the x, y coordinates? I think the reason why I am struggling to visualize using just the image3D(mse, ~x*y, mz = 637) command is because there are many x and y coordinate duplicates that correspond to the z axis coordinates.
2) If there is no way to get around this, is there a way to eliminate the z coordinates and reduce the duplicate x and y coordinates to properly visualize my 2D ion images and extract relevant mass spectra?

Thank you in advance!
Alena

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alena,

I would try setting the z value to NULL:
coord(mse)$z <- NULL
or
subset your object by z values.

This way you should be able to image 637:

image3D(mse, ~x*y, mz = 637)

I hope this works/helps

Hey David!

Thank you for your suggestion! This worked so well, I'm able to visualize my data now. This is the full code that I used:

coord(mse)$z <- NULL
mse1 <- mse[,!duplicated(coord(mse))]
image(mse1, ~x*y, mz=637.2, plusminus=0.2)

I didn't try to subset the data but it may be something I try in the future if I want to access the z coordinates.
